name: Fort St. George
label: Fort St. George
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Fort St. George' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Fort St. George'.
notes: The first English fortress in India, now the state secretariat.

text.description:
Fort St. George is where Chennai began. The English East India Company bought the coastal land in 1639 and finished the fort on 23 April 1644, St George's Day, which gave it its name. It was the first English fortress in India, and the city grew up around it. Today it is a working government complex. It holds the Tamil Nadu legislative assembly and secretariat, and the Fort Museum and St. Mary's Church are inside.

From outside, the fort photographs best as a classic exterior: thick walls about 6 metres high, the gateway and the colonial facade, all seen across the open approach from Rajaji Salai. The open space lets you step back and fit the whole frontage into one picture without cropping the edges. Inside the fort stands a teakwood flagstaff, 46 metres tall and one of the tallest in the country.

A phone does this subject well because the scene is mostly wide, even and architectural. Take one wide frame to show the whole fort, then move closer for details such as the gateway arch or the texture of the walls. Aim for morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and the walls look warmer. If you have time, Napier Bridge is a recommended additional spot, with its white arches over the Cooum River.
text.geographic_location: Fort St. George stands on Chennai's coast. George Town grew out of the settlement that developed around the fort. The approach road is Rajaji Salai. Napier Bridge is a recommended additional spot.
text.directions_text: No Underground, rail or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Fort St. George area on Rajaji Salai, by taxi or hired scooter from wherever you are in Chennai. The phone icon on the map is about 3 minutes on foot from the fort, with the fort to the east of you. Walk east towards the walls and gateway. The phone icon on the map is about 200 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole frontage. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close and cannot fit the walls in. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the gateway or wall details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 200 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. George's walls, in the entrance zone off Rajaji Salai. The fort lies to the east of you. From here you see the walls, the gateway and the colonial facade, framed against the open approach from Rajaji Salai.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the base of the walls up with a horizontal grid line so the fort does not lean. Leave a little open ground in the foreground to give a sense of scale. Then take a closer shot of the gateway on its own. For a different view, Napier Bridge is a recommended additional spot, with its white arches over the Cooum River, and the waterfront and river banks alongside.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the facade to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky does not wash out and the walls keep their colour. Avoid digital zoom beyond your phone's telephoto lens, as it softens the detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon, when the light is soft.

text.access_note: The fort is an active government complex, so some areas are closed and you may need photo ID at security, and the Fort Museum inside is ticketed; check the official site and any posted photography signs before you go.

name: Marina Beach
label: Marina Beach
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Chennai Lighthouse' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Chennai Lighthouse' (way/1552618806): middle (29 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/22902280: large area 'Marina Beach' (3203 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Long urban beach along the Bay of Bengal, best at sunrise.

text.description: Marina Beach is a long, wide, sandy city beach on the Bay of Bengal, and it is where Chennai comes to stroll, fly kites and cool off in the evening. It is a natural beach that runs south from near Fort St. George, with an average width of about 300 m. That width is why it photographs so well: there is a lot of open sand and sea, with the city lined up behind it. The promenade was laid out in 1884 by the then governor, Mount Stuart Elphinstone Grant Duff, and statues and memorials were added along it over the years, including the Triumph of Labour and a Gandhi statue. It is one of the busiest beaches in the country, with around 30,000 visitors on a weekday and about 50,000 at weekends and on holidays. Swimming is legally prohibited because of the strong undercurrent, so photograph from the sand or the promenade rather than the water. The best overall picture comes from the Chennai Lighthouse observation gallery, near the south end of the beach. Time at the top is short, so have your phone ready and your framing in mind before you step out. If the lighthouse is closed or crowded, go down to the sand and shoot back towards the lighthouse, which suits a sunrise scene with the sea in front.
text.geographic_location: Marina Beach runs along Chennai's Bay of Bengal shoreline, south of Fort St. George. The lighthouse viewpoint is near the southern end of the beach.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot, so go by taxi or hired scooter to the Chennai Lighthouse, near the south end of Marina Beach. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole beach, sea and skyline from the deck. Use the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view of the shoreline. Try the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out groups of people, kites or the statues on the promenade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Chennai Lighthouse (observation gallery near the south end of Marina Beach). A panoramic view from the top of the Marina, showing the whole length of the beach, the Bay of Bengal and the city skyline. The beach spot on the map lies to the north of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the shoreline up with one of the horizontal lines so the curve of the beach leads the eye away from you. Leave about a third of the frame for sky and sea. For a different view, go down to Marina Beach itself and shoot a wide sunrise scene with the lighthouse behind and the Bay of Bengal in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Time at the top is short, so open the camera and turn on gridlines before you step out. Tap the brightest part of the sky to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sea and clouds keep their colour. Try a panorama along the shoreline, holding the phone steady and moving slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Some visitors recommend sunset or evening, and others note that morning gives the clearest views. The beach is busier at weekends and on holidays, so a weekday morning is the quieter option.

text.access_note: The beach is an open public space, but the lighthouse viewing gallery is a paid, ticketed lift ride, so check on the day for opening hours and fees.
claims_not_in_sources: The coast at Chennai faces east, so the sun rises over the sea when seen from the beach.
Gridlines and a small drop in exposure help a bright sky and sea keep their colour in phone photos.
A weekday morning is likely to be quieter at the beach than a weekend, based on the visitor numbers given.
From the lighthouse deck the ultra-wide lens will fit more of the beach and skyline into the frame than the default lens (1x).

name: Government Museum, Chennai
label: Government Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Pantheon Road' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Pantheon Road nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1126975457: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Chennai Government Museum' (216 m across).

text.description:
The Government Museum in Egmore is a colonial-era museum complex that can be photographed from the public road. It started in 1851, making it the second oldest museum in India, and it moved to its present site on Pantheon Road in 1854. The complex covers around 16 acres, with six buildings and 46 galleries. It also holds the Connemara Public Library and the National Art Gallery.

The simplest picture is taken from the public road, with no ticket needed. From there you can frame the old museum building and its facade from outside the complex. The middle of the complex lies a short walk to the north-west of that spot.

Inside the gates, the Museum Theatre is the other building to know about. It is a rare Italianate-style structure, built in the late 19th century. It has a high plinth, a tall flight of steps and a verandah of columns joined by rounded arches. You need an entry ticket to reach it, so treat it as an optional extra, or use it as a second viewpoint if you go in. Camera rules inside the museum can vary, so check the official site before you go. Morning or late afternoon gives softer light on the stonework.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in the Government Museum Complex on Pantheon Road in Egmore, central Chennai. It shares the complex with the Connemara Public Library and the National Art Gallery.
text.directions_text: Navigate to Pantheon Road in Egmore and ask for the Government Museum. Get out at the main museum frontage on the road. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the facade as the eye sees it. If you are standing close to the frontage, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit more of the building in. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out architectural detail without stepping into the road.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Pantheon Road (in front of the main museum frontage). The colonial-era museum building and its facade, framed from the public road outside the complex. The middle of the complex lies to the north-west of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the building's vertical edges with them so the walls do not lean. Leave a little sky above the roofline and keep your phone level. If you go inside the ticketed complex, the Italianate Museum Theatre is a good alternative subject, with its steps and arched verandah.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Check the lens is clean before you shoot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer.

text.access_note: The view from Pantheon Road is public, but the museum complex and the Museum Theatre are ticketed, and photography rules inside vary, so check the official site before you go.

name: Chennai Central railway station
label: Chennai Central
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Poonamallee High Road' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Vepery High Road' (roads).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/2481969291: the OpenStreetMap point 'Puratchi Thalaivar Dr. M. G. Ramachandran Central'.

text.description: Chennai Central is the city's grand railway terminus, and its brick-red front is one of the most recognisable buildings in Chennai. The station opened in 1873 to a design by George Harding. Robert Chisholm later reworked it, adding the central clock tower and the caps on the main towers, and that work was finished in 1900. The style mixes Gothic Revival and Romanesque Revival, so you get pointed details, strong towers and a long, busy frontage. The clock tower is the tallest part, at about 136 ft. The building is officially a heritage building. In 2019 the station was renamed after M. G. Ramachandran, and a 100 ft flag mast was put up in front of the main building the same year. It photographs well because the whole facade can be seen from the road, with the towers lined up against the sky and the daily bustle of the forecourt in front. That makes it a good place for a record of the city rather than a quiet, empty shot. Take the wide view first, then move in for a tighter picture of the clock tower or the towers. It is a working station, so keep clear of entrances and passenger routes, and stop for a moment if the crowd builds up. Casual photos are generally fine, but professional shoots may need permission, so check the rules before you go.
text.geographic_location: Chennai Central is in the Park Town area of central Chennai, in the Periamet neighbourhood. It stands where Poonamallee High Road, Pallavan Salai and Wall Tax Road meet, next to the Moore Market Complex.
text.directions_text: Aim for Park Town in central Chennai and head for the station's main entrance on Poonamallee High Road. For the full-front view, walk east along Poonamallee High Road towards the station and settle on the forecourt side, opposite the main entrance. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Once you are on the forecourt side of Poonamallee High Road, opposite the main entrance, start with the default lens (1x), which should take in most of the facade. If the towers are cut off at the sides, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). Use 2x or more on the telephoto for a close picture of the clock tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Poonamallee High Road (opposite the main entrance, on the forecourt side of the station). The full front facade of the station, with its Gothic Revival and Romanesque-style frontage framed from the road. This is the standard postcard angle.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Centre the clock tower and let the two main towers sit evenly either side, with the road and forecourt at the bottom of the frame. Wait for a gap in the traffic and people to get a cleaner foreground. For a tighter alternative, zoom in on the clock tower and the brick-red walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Turn on gridlines and line up the towers with the vertical lines so they do not lean. Tap the brick-red wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright and washing out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the brickwork, and the forecourt is often quieter early in the day.

text.access_note: The forecourt and road are public, but this is a working station, so check the official site or station notices for photography rules before you go, and do not block passengers.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the brickwork.
The forecourt is often quieter early in the day.
The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) may be needed to fit the whole facade in from the road.

name: M. A. Chidambaram Stadium
label: Chepauk Stadium
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Marina Beach' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Marina Beach' (way/22902280): edge nearest the subject (3187 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/60961: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'MA Chidambaram Stadium' (324 m across).
notes: Famous cricket ground, home of Chennai Super Kings.

text.description:
M. A. Chidambaram Stadium, usually called Chepauk, is Chennai's big cricket ground and home of the Chennai Super Kings. It dates from 1916 and is the second oldest international cricket stadium in India still in use, after Eden Gardens in Kolkata. It hosted its first Test in 1934, and rebuilding work has taken the capacity to around 38,000. The stands, roofs and floodlights give it a strong shape, and it looks best from outside after dark.

The suggested photo is taken from Marina Beach, at the northern end toward the Gandhi statue area. This works best once the floodlights are on in the evening. You are photographing a glow and a skyline, not architectural detail, so keep the frame simple: some foreground of beach or trees, and the lit stadium behind.

The best-known views, such as the Anna Pavilion and the upper stands, are inside the ground and need a match ticket. If you want a second outside angle, Chepauk MRTS Station is said to give a broad view across much of the stadium from the elevated platform. That tip is quite old, so check that the view is still open to visitors. On match days, expect crowds and possible closures near Wallajah Road.
text.geographic_location: The stadium is in Chepauk, Chennai, a short walk inland (west) of Marina Beach. The photo spot is at the northern end of the beach, toward the Gandhi statue area.
text.directions_text: Head for the northern end of Marina Beach, toward the Gandhi statue area. If you plan to be here on a match day, allow extra time, as crowds and closures near Wallajah Road may slow you down. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so you keep the beach, the treeline and the glow in one frame. Try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the stadium lights closer, and use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Marina Beach (northern end, toward the Gandhi statue area). The stadium's floodlit glow rising above the beach treeline and the sea.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the glow on one of the upper lines, with trees or beach lower in the frame. Keep your phone level so the horizon stays straight. For a different angle, the elevated Chepauk MRTS Station is suggested as a way to see across the stadium, if that view is still open.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Use night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a railing for the few seconds it needs. Tap on the bright lights, then lower the exposure slider a little so the floodlights do not turn into a white blur.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: After the floodlights come on in the evening.

text.access_note: Marina Beach is an open public space, but the stadium's inside views need a match ticket, and photography rules inside are unknown, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Floodlights may be on mainly during evening matches or events, so check the fixture list if you want a lit stadium.
Telephoto brings the stadium lights closer in the frame, and the stadium is a long way from the viewpoint.
Holding the phone steady against your body or a railing helps night mode give a sharper result.
Marina Beach is an open public space.

name: Kapaleeshwarar Temple
label: Kapaleeshwarar Temple
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Mylapore Tank' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Mylapore Tank' (node/410614397): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/21203725: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Kapaleeshwarar Temple' (335 m across).

text.description:
Kapaleeshwarar Temple is a Hindu temple to Shiva in Mylapore, Chennai. The temple you see today dates from around the 17th century. Its tall gopuram (gateway tower) was built in 1906 and stands about 120 ft high, covered in painted stucco figures. The temple has an older story too. Tamil poet-saints praised it as far back as the 7th century, and it is thought to have first stood nearer the seashore. Right beside it lies the temple tank, known as the Mylapore Tank, about 190 m long and 143 m wide. It holds water all year, and a 16-pillared stone mandapam stands in the middle.

The tank side is a recommended place to photograph from. The view across the water towards the gopuram is a good angle to aim for, and when the water is still the tower may be reflected in the tank. This angle is usually quieter than the busy front of the temple and gives a cleaner view of the tower. You are also less likely to have power lines cutting through the frame. Early morning is the time to aim for, because the water is calmest then. If you want the full height of the tower with its tiers of figures filling the picture, the front of the temple is the other classic view, though it can be crowded. Keep to the outer compound and the tank edge for photos, as photography is restricted in worship areas.
text.geographic_location: The temple is in Mylapore, Chennai.
text.directions_text: Start from Mylapore itself, the neighbourhood around the temple, and go by taxi or hired scooter. Ask to be dropped at the Mylapore Tank (Kapaleeshwarar Tank). If you have trouble reaching the tank edge, walk around to the eastern side of the tank, which is usually the open part. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole scene: tank, gopuram and reflection. Switch to telephoto (2x or 3x, depending on your phone) to bring the tower closer and fill the frame. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of sky and water, because the tower will look small.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (southwest corner of the tank, or the far side opposite the gopuram). The gopuram seen across the tank, often with its reflection in the still water. The southwest corner or the far side of the tank is a suggested alternative, but check that it is reachable.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the water's edge on the lower line so the reflection gets plenty of room. Keep the tower upright in the frame and tilt the phone as little as you can, so the tower doesn't lean. If you want the full height of the east gopuram with its painted figures filling the frame, walk round to the temple front as a second viewpoint.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the gopuram to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky does not wash out and the colours of the tower stay rich. Wait a moment for ripples to settle before taking the photo. A Live Photo can help you pick the calmest frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the water is still and the reflection is clearest. Friday and festival days can be crowded.

text.access_note: The temple is an active place of worship where photography is not allowed in the sanctum and is restricted in worship areas, and the tank may not be reachable from every side, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Modest dress is usually expected when visiting a Hindu temple.
Tilting the phone upwards makes tall buildings look as if they lean inwards.
Gridlines help keep the tower upright and the water level in the frame.
A Live Photo lets you choose the calmest moment on rippled water.

name: Chennai Egmore railway station
label: Egmore Station
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Chennai Egmore railway station' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/5275790188: the OpenStreetMap point 'Chennai Egmore'.

text.description:
Chennai Egmore is a working railway station, and it is also a notable Indo-Saracenic building. The terminal building was designed by the British architects Henry Irwin and E. C. Bird. Construction began in September 1905, and it opened to the public on 11 June 1908. It is built in the Indo-Saracenic style, with Gothic and Dravidian touches. A large dome sits above a three-span roof, and the pillars and brackets carry carved motifs based on temple architecture. Brick, granite and sandstone are used together, so the building has a contrasting appearance.

The building is long, about 91 metres by 21 metres, and the station sits between two flyovers on Gandhi-Irwin Road. That makes it hard to fit the whole front into one frame from close up. Start with a wide shot of the facade, then move in for details such as the dome, the carved pillars and the brackets. Stay clear of the entrances and walkways, as this is a busy station. Personal photography is generally allowed, but keep out of passengers' way. Commercial shoots may need permission.
text.geographic_location: In the Egmore neighbourhood of central Chennai, on Gandhi-Irwin Road, with a rear entrance on Poonamallee High Road.
text.directions_text: Egmore metro station on the Green Line of the Chennai Metro serves the railway station, so that is the easiest way to arrive without a car. Otherwise go by taxi or autorickshaw to Gandhi-Irwin Road in Egmore and ask for the main entrance. The phone icon on the map is at the front of the building, so there is no further walk once you arrive. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to get as much of the long facade and dome into the frame as you can. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of the entrance. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the dome, carved pillars and the mix of brick and stone.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here your photo shows the Indo-Saracenic facade, the reason many visitors shoot here.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: The whole building is hard to fit in from directly in front of it. Take a few steps back, switch on the gridlines and keep the verticals straight, or try panorama mode, moving slowly and keeping the phone level. Then take closer shots of the dome and the carved details. Keep clear of entrances so you don't obstruct passengers.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky doesn't wash out and the brick colours stay rich. Use the gridlines to keep the lines of the building straight.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually shows off the brick and stone best. Midday sun is harsher and flatter on the facade.

text.access_note: The station is a working public railway station with security staff and CCTV, so check the official site before you go for any rules on photography, especially anything beyond personal snapshots.
claims_not_in_sources: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters brick and stone facades, while midday sun is harsher.
Panorama mode and the ultra-wide lens help fit a long building into one frame when you cannot step far back.
The station is busy with passengers, so photographers should keep clear of entrances.

name: Elliot's Beach
label: Elliot's Beach
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Karl Schmidt Memorial' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Kaj Schmidt Memorial' (pois); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/14304132: large area 'Elliots Beach' (3380 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description: Elliot's Beach, also known as Besant Nagar Beach or simply "the Bessie", is a long, open city beach just south of Marina Beach. It is named after Edward Elliot, a chief magistrate and superintendent of police of the Madras Presidency. For a phone photo, the best anchor is the Kaj Schmidt Memorial. It honours a Danish sailor who lost his life trying to save a girl from drowning. Its lighthouse-like silhouette stands out well against a darkening sky, and it gives the picture a bit of history in the foreground. Behind it you get the Bay of Bengal, the sand and usually a few people strolling or paddling, which adds scale and life. The Shrine of Our Lady of Good Health stands on the shore, and the Ashtalakshmi Temple, built in 1976, is near the southern end. The temple is a good second picture: its gopuram and carved entrance framed against the skyline, with the sea nearby. Weekends and evenings can be busy, so if you want a clean frame without crowds, go early in the morning. Keep your phone dry and your feet back from the waves: the monsoon months (June to September) are described as less safe on the beach, so keep back from the water.
text.geographic_location: In Besant Nagar, in the south of Chennai, on the shore of the Bay of Bengal. It sits next to the southern tip of Marina Beach.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops close to this spot, so head for Besant Nagar and then go to the shore. Once on the beach, look for the Kaj Schmidt Memorial. The beach itself is a long stretch, so use the memorial to find your place. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the memorial, the sea and the sky all sit comfortably in one frame. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more sky at dusk. A touch of telephoto (2x) works well for picking out beachgoers near the waterline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject. The memorial in the foreground with the Bay of Bengal and the beach behind it, often with beachgoers and a twilight sky. Wait for a few people to walk through the background for a sense of life and scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place the memorial on one of the vertical lines, leaving the other two-thirds for sea and sky. Crouch a little so the memorial rises against the sky. For something different, walk to the Ashtalakshmi Temple near the southern end of the beach and frame its gopuram and carved entrance against the skyline.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the memorial to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the twilight sky keeps its colour and the memorial becomes a clean silhouette. After sunset, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body, as the sand is soft and it is hard to stay still.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: From about 5:30 pm to 7:00 pm for twilight, with beachgoers in the scene. For an empty beach, try sunrise instead.

text.access_note: The beach itself is an open public space; the church and the temple nearby are places of worship, so dress modestly and check opening times locally if you plan to go inside.

name: Madras High Court
label: Madras High Court
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rajaji Salai' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Rajaji Salai nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/34326333: large area 'Madras High Court' (643 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Indo-Saracenic court complex with a domed tower.

text.description: The Madras High Court is a big Indo-Saracenic building, with domes, arches and towers, and it is one of the largest court complexes in the world by area. Building began in October 1888, and it was officially opened on 12 July 1892. J. W. Brassington designed it, and it was later expanded under Henry Irwin. A lighthouse already stood on the site and was raised to 175 ft (53 m) during the works, so a tall tower sits among the domes. The building photographs well because of its detail: the ornamental façade, the rhythm of the arches and the skyline of domes. The interior and grounds are restricted, so the road outside is the practical place to take your photo. Confirm the exact spot on the map before you set up. Keep the whole façade in one frame for a classic view, then step in for the domes and carved details. Traffic and street furniture can get in the way, so wait for a gap and keep your phone level. Works outside the court have been reported to spoil the view at times, so be ready to adjust your angle. Photography inside the campus is restricted, so enjoy the building from the pavement.
text.geographic_location: The court is in the George Town area of central Chennai, on Rajaji Salai near Parry's Corner and close to the harbour.
text.directions_text: Head for Parry's Corner in George Town and follow Rajaji Salai; if you are coming from further away, go by taxi or hired scooter. Check the map as you go, because the exact spot is best confirmed there. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Rajaji Salai. The Indo-Saracenic façade and domes of the court seen from the road outside the campus.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the building up with them so the towers stay upright. Include a little sky above the domes, and wait for a gap in the traffic or passers-by. If the ultra-wide lens makes the building lean, step back or use 1x instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap a well-lit part of the façade to focus. Then pull the exposure slider down slightly so the sky does not wash out and the domes keep their detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows on the façade.

name: San Thome Basilica
label: San Thome Basilica
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'San Thome Basilica' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1115403900: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St. Thomas Cathedral Basilica' (78 m across).
notes: Neo-Gothic church built over the tomb of St. Thomas.

text.description:
San Thome Basilica is the white Neo-Gothic church of the Santhome neighbourhood, and it is the cathedral of the Archdiocese of Madras-Mylapore. The Portuguese built a church here over the traditional tomb of Saint Thomas the Apostle, which opened in 1523. The British rebuilt it in Gothic Revival style, and it was consecrated in 1896. That rebuilt look is what you photograph today: pale walls, pointed details and two spires. The main spire stands at the left of the entrance, is about 45 metres tall and works as the bell tower. A second spire rises from the centre of the church to mark the believed position of the tomb.

The façade photographs best from the main entrance area on Santhome High Road. There is open space in front of the church, so you can step back and fit the whole width and both towers into one frame. Early morning or late afternoon is kinder to the white walls than harsh midday sun. Weekday mornings are usually calmer than Sundays and Mass times, when the forecourt gets busy. Keep your phone upright and level so the towers don't lean. If you go inside, photography is only allowed in some areas, so follow the signs, switch the flash off and be discreet during services.
text.geographic_location: In the Santhome neighbourhood of Chennai, on Santhome High Road.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground or tram stops listed for this spot, so head for the Santhome neighbourhood of Chennai and ask for San Thome Basilica on Santhome High Road. Once you arrive, go to the front of the church; the phone icon on the map is at the basilica, and the main entrance area on Santhome High Road gives the best full-width view. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close to the entrance and want both spires and the full width in one frame. Use the default lens (1x) if you can step back into the open space in front for a more natural look. The telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is useful for the top of the main spire or the façade details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Use the main entrance area and the open space in front on Santhome High Road to frame the façade, so you can capture the white Neo-Gothic front with its spires.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line up the church so the vertical lines of the towers run parallel to the grid. Keep the phone upright and level, not tilted up, to stop the towers leaning inwards. Leave a little space above the spires. For a second shot, move a few steps back into the open space in front and try the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more balanced view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the façade to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a touch so the white walls keep their detail and don't turn pale and flat. Don't use flash inside, and only photograph where it is allowed.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and the white façade stands out. Weekday mornings are quieter than Sundays and Mass times.

text.access_note: This is a working church and place of worship; photography inside is allowed only in some areas, so follow any signs and check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Weekday mornings are generally less crowded than Sundays and Mass times.
Early morning or late afternoon light is softer and suits the white façade.

name: Vivekanandar Illam
label: Vivekanandar Illam
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kamarajar Salai' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Kamarajar Salai nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/211772507: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Vivekanandar Illam' (159 m across).
notes: Red heritage building facing Marina Beach.

text.description:
Vivekanandar Illam is a white, semi-circular Victorian building on Chennai's Marina promenade, facing the beach and the Bay of Bengal across the road. It was built in 1842 by Frederic Tudor to store ice, and was later known as Castle Kernan. Swami Vivekananda stayed here for about a week in February 1897, and in 1963 the building was renamed in his honour. Today it is run by Ramakrishna Math and holds an exhibition on his life.

It photographs well because the front is plain, pale and curved, so it stands out against the sky. The best view is the whole facade from the beach side of Kamarajar Salai, looking at the building's front. The road is busy, so wait for a gap in the traffic and keep your phone steady. Start with the default lens (1x) and step back until the whole building fits, with a little sky above the roofline. If you can't step back far enough, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x), but keep the phone level so the walls don't lean. For a second picture, Vivekananda Park gives you the building across the green space, with the statue in the foreground. Take any interior photos only if the current rules allow it, so check before you go in.
text.geographic_location: On the Marina promenade road (Kamarajar Salai) in central Chennai, facing Marina Beach and the Bay of Bengal.
text.directions_text: Head for the Marina Beach seafront in central Chennai and follow the promenade road until you see the white, curved building facing the sea. If you are coming from elsewhere in the city, ask locally for Vivekanandar Illam on Kamarajar Salai. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole facade. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if traffic or railings stop you stepping back, and the telephoto (2x or more) for details such as the curved front and windows.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Kamarajar Salai (beach side of the road, facing the building's front). The white, semi-circular Victorian facade of Vivekanandar Illam with the Marina Beach behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the roofline level, with the building centred and a band of sky above it. Keep the phone straight rather than tilting it up, so the walls stay upright. If you want an alternative, Vivekananda Park shows the building across the green space with the Vivekananda statue in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white walls keep their detail against the bright sky. Take a few shots between passing vehicles.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning is likely to be kinder to the white front, because the sun will be behind you. Midday sun will make the walls look harsh and flat.

text.access_note: The road and the outside of the building can be photographed from public ground, but opening days and photography rules inside the exhibition vary, so check the official site before you go.

name: Parthasarathy Temple, Triplicane
label: Parthasarathy Temple
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Beach Road' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Beach Road nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1080608337: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Sri Parthasarathy Koil' (155 m across).

text.description:
Parthasarathy Temple is a Vishnu temple in the Triplicane (Thiruvallikeni) neighbourhood, and it is one of the oldest structures in Chennai. Its roots go back to the Pallava period. The Cholas later added to it, and the Vijayanagara kings expanded it further in the 15th and 16th centuries. The name means 'charioteer of Arjuna', and the main deity is Krishna shown with a moustache, which is unusual. The temple also has shrines to other forms of Vishnu, including Narasimha, Rama and Ranganatha. Its towers and pillared halls are covered in carvings.

For a phone photo, the best view is the eastern gateway (the eastern thoranam entrance) from Beach Road. The carved entrance is a clear subject of its own, and you can shoot it from the street without going inside. From there you will see only the general approach towards the complex, so walk west to the eastern entrance to frame the gateway and its carvings. Keep the gateway central and use the gridlines to keep the verticals straight. Then move closer, or zoom in, for the carved detail. Traffic and people will pass through the frame, so wait a moment for a gap.

Photography is not allowed in the inner sanctum or around the deity. Phones are fine in the outer areas. Check current darshan times before you go, and allow for festival-time crowds and road closures.
text.geographic_location: The temple is in the Triplicane (Thiruvallikeni) neighbourhood of Chennai. The viewpoint is on Beach Road, on the temple's eastern side, about 500 m east of the gate.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Triplicane and Beach Road by taxi or hired scooter. The temple's east gate and main complex are to the west of it, about 500-600 m on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Once you have walked west to the eastern entrance, stay at 1x for the whole gateway. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the carvings only from there, as they cannot be resolved from where you stand. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you end up very close to the gate and cannot fit it in.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Beach Road (eastern thoranam entrance, facing the temple's east gate). The temple's eastern gateway and entrance carvings, framed from the street outside the complex. From here you will see only the general approach towards the temple.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: At the eastern entrance, turn on the gridlines and line the gateway up with the centre of the frame. Hold the phone level so the tower does not lean. Take one wide shot with the street in front as foreground, then a closer zoomed shot of the carvings. Wait for a gap in the traffic and passers-by.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the gateway to focus. Then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out the carvings.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is a sensible choice, when the street is quieter and the light is softer. Avoid festival days if you want a clear view of the gate.

text.access_note: This is an active place of worship, and photography is prohibited in the inner sanctum and around the deity but allowed in the outer precincts, so check current darshan times and any festival-time crowds or road closures before you go.

name: Valluvar Kottam
label: Valluvar Kottam
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Valluvar Kottam' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Valluvar Kottam' (way/209535268): middle (345 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/209535268: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Valluvar Kottam' (347 m across).
notes: Stone temple-chariot monument to the poet Thiruvalluvar.

text.description: Valluvar Kottam is a memorial to the classical Tamil poet-philosopher Valluvar, and its centrepiece is a 39-metre stone chariot that looks like a temple car. It is a copy of the famous temple chariot of Thiruvarur, built from around 3000 blocks of granite, with four huge wheels and a statue of Valluvar inside. Underneath, carvings show all 133 chapters of the Kural, and the Kural Manimandapa inscribes its 1,330 couplets. The memorial was opened in April 1976. It photographs well because the chariot is a single, bold shape that stands clear of the trees and rooftops around it. One visitor guide recommends the northeast corner of the garden for a full view against open sky, so that is worth a look too. The grey stone, the carved wheels and the painted detail all show up well when the sky behind is clear. If you want a closer, more detailed shot, walk to the front and photograph the chariot head-on with the engraved Kural panels around it. A third option is the terrace, where the statue mandapam rises above the roofline, especially when the evening lighting is on. Please don't climb or lean on the monument. Weekends can bring crowds and exhibitions that block the view, so a weekday morning is easier.
text.geographic_location: Valluvar Kottam is in the Nungambakkam neighbourhood of Chennai, at the junction of Kodambakkam High Road and Village Road. The monument stands on ground that was once the deepest part of the old Nungambakkam lake.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is given for this spot, so head for Nungambakkam and aim for the junction of Kodambakkam High Road and Village Road. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from where you stand, which fits the whole chariot against the sky without distortion. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close to the front and want the whole chariot and the panels in one shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Valluvar Kottam (northeast corner of the garden). The whole chariot structure framed against the sky, taken from the garden's far corner. From here the chariot is straight ahead to the north, framed against open sky. If you want a second view, the front plaza gives a head-on shot of the chariot with the Kural panels, and the terrace shows the statue mandapam rising above the roofline.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the chariot's base on a lower line so the sky fills the top. Keep the phone level so the tall sides don't lean inwards. Wait for people to move out of the foreground, or use them to show scale. For the head-on alternative, use the ultra-wide (0.5x) and keep the phone straight and centred.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stone to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky stays blue and the carved detail isn't washed out. In the evening, with the lights on, try night mode and hold the phone steady against a wall or railing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, roughly 7:00 to 9:00 AM, is recommended for cooler temperatures and softer light. Weekday mornings are likely to be quieter than weekends.

text.access_note: Entry rules for the grounds and for climbing the chariot may vary or be restricted, so check the official site before you go.

name: Ripon Building
label: Ripon Building
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ripon Building' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q3521669: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description:
The Ripon Building is the headquarters of the Greater Chennai Corporation, and it is one of the easiest big buildings in the city to photograph. It is an all-white neoclassical block that mixes Ionic and Corinthian styles. A tall clock tower stands in the middle of the front, so the whole facade is nicely symmetrical. From the lawn in front you see the white frontage and the tower framed by open grass and the statue of Lord Ripon, with nothing much in the way.

The building was commissioned in 1909 and designed by G.T.S. Harris. It is named after Lord Ripon, who is remembered as the father of local self-government. It is about 85 metres long, and the central tower rises to 43 metres. The clock face is 2.5 metres across, and the Westminster Quarter chiming clock was installed in 1913. Look up at the tower once you have the wide shot, because the clock is the detail that makes the picture.

This is a working government office, so plan on photographing it from outside. Photography inside is restricted. Another good frame is from Periyar Bridge, where the clock tower can sit in the same shot as Victoria Public Hall and Central Station. Early morning or late afternoon is the best time to go. Step back as far as the lawn allows so the whole front fits, and wait for a gap if people walk across.
text.geographic_location: In central Chennai, close to Chennai Central railway station. It sits at the front of the Greater Chennai Corporation's office complex.
text.directions_text: Start from Chennai Central railway station, which is the nearest well-known landmark, and go on by taxi or hired scooter to the Ripon Building. The building is a large white structure with a central clock tower, so it is easy to recognise when you get close. Walk onto the lawn in front of the facade to reach the phone icon on the map. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole white facade and the clock tower together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and cannot fit the full width. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the clock face and the top of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the white neoclassical front and its central clock tower are framed by the open lawn and the statue of Lord Ripon.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the clock tower up with the centre line so the symmetry works. Keep the phone level and upright so the walls and columns stay straight. Include a little lawn or the statue in the foreground for depth. If you want a wider city view, Periyar Bridge is an alternative that puts the clock tower in the same frame as Victoria Public Hall and Central Station.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the white wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white facade keeps its detail and does not turn pale. Take a few shots in case people walk through the frame.

text.access_note: The building is a working government office and is best photographed from outside, so check the official site before you go for any visit rules.
claims_not_in_sources: Keeping the phone level helps the walls and columns look straight, while the ultra-wide lens can stretch or tilt the edges of the building if the phone is angled upwards.
Lowering the exposure slider can help stop a white building from looking washed out in bright light.
People may walk across the lawn in front of the building, so you may need to wait for a clear view.

name: Theosophical Society Adyar
label: Theosophical Society

notes: Green estate with a giant banyan tree on the Adyar river.

text.description: The Theosophical Society's international headquarters sits in Adyar, a district of Chennai. The Society was founded in New York on 17 November 1875 and moved its headquarters to Adyar in 1882, when Helena Blavatsky and Henry Steel Olcott made the journey from New York. Today it is best thought of as a green, calm compound rather than a single building. Part of it is known as Olcott Gardens, and a 10-acre wooded area there was set aside as a scout camping centre. That makes it a pleasant place for a quiet photo walk, with tall trees, shaded paths and a gentle, unhurried feel that is quite different from the busy streets around it. For a phone, the best pictures are usually of tree-lined paths, dappled light on the ground and any older buildings you pass, rather than one grand view. Look for a path or an avenue of trees that leads the eye into the picture, and keep a little foreground, such as leaves or a bench, to give depth. The grounds are an institution's own space, so be discreet, keep your voice low and do not photograph people without asking. Rules on entry and photography can change, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The compound is in Adyar, an area of Chennai, India. It is the home of the Theosophical Society's international headquarters.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Adyar area of Chennai and go by taxi or hired scooter. Ask to be dropped as close as you can to the Theosophical Society grounds. The phone icon on the map is about 420 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for paths, trees and buildings. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for a long avenue of trees, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as bark, leaves or carved and painted features.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 420 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. Walk north-east towards the subject and take your photos looking along the paths as the grounds open up in front of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place a path or line of trunks along one of the lines so it leads into the frame. Keep a little foreground, such as leaves or a bench, for depth. Hold the phone level so tall trunks stay straight.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the scene, then slide the exposure down a little so bright sky does not wash out. Under dense shade, tap on a mid-tone patch instead. Use portrait mode only for close subjects such as leaves or a detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, more flattering light under the trees than the harsh midday sun.

text.access_note: This is the working headquarters of an organisation, so entry and photography rules may apply: check the official site before you go.

name: Armenian Church, Chennai
label: Armenian Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Armenian Street' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Armenian Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1076727642: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Armenian Church of the Virgin Mary' (41 m across).

text.description:
The Armenian Church of the Virgin Mary (St Mary's) is one of the oldest churches in the Indian subcontinent. It was built in 1712 and rebuilt in 1772, in George Town, where Armenian merchants once traded silk, spices and gems. From the street it is a modest, low building, and its charm lies in the quiet compound around it: a leafy courtyard, old headstones (about 350 Armenians are buried here) and a belfry beside the church holding six bells. The bells range from 21 to 26 inches and are believed to be the largest and heaviest in Chennai. Two of them were cast in London in 1837.

For a phone photo, the simplest shot is the front of the church and its entrance, taken from Armenian Street with the High Court buildings behind. Inside the gate, the belfry and the headstones among the trees make calmer, more atmospheric pictures. Photography inside the church building is reported as not allowed, so keep to the exterior and courtyard. A newer Catholic church stands right beside the old one and can confuse the view from the street, so check that the building in your frame is the right one. The area is busy and parking is hard to find, so travelling light and arriving on foot works best.
text.geographic_location: The church is on Armenian Street in George Town, in the older, busy neighbourhood of George Town in Chennai, directly opposite the High Court side.
text.directions_text: Head for George Town and the High Court area and ask for Armenian Street. Parking nearby is difficult, so it is easier to be dropped off. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the front of the church and gate. If the lane feels tight, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole building in. Use telephoto (2x or more) inside the compound for the belfry and details on the headstones.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Armenian Street (directly in front of the church gate, opposite the High Court side). The church's front facade and entrance framed by the lane, with the High Court complex nearby in the background.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the church centred with the gate in the lower part of the frame. Hold the phone level so the walls do not lean. Make sure the older church is your subject and not the newer Catholic church beside it. As an alternative, go through the gate and photograph the six-bell belfry beside the church, or the old headstones with the church behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the church wall to set focus and drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the facade stays detailed. Inside the compound, tap on the headstones to focus and use portrait mode only if you want the church softly blurred behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go in the morning, when the street should be quieter. On Sundays the bells are rung around 9:30 am, but photographing the bells may be restricted and the belfry is often locked, so do not plan a shot around it.

text.access_note: This is a heritage church with a compound and graveyard, and visiting times seem to vary, so check on arrival; photography inside the church building is not allowed.
claims_not_in_sources: The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) may help in the narrow street in front of the church.
The street is likely to be quieter in the morning than later in the day.
Setting exposure for a bright sky can help keep the facade detailed.

name: Senate House (University of Madras)
label: Senate House
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kamarajar Salai' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Kamarajar Salai nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/23894473: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Senate House' (110 m across).
notes: Indo-Saracenic hall of the University of Madras.

text.description:
The Senate House is the administrative centre of the University of Madras, and it stands right on the Marina seafront. Robert Chisholm built it between 1874 and 1879, and it is considered one of the best and oldest examples of Indo-Saracenic architecture in India, with some Byzantine touches mixed in. For a phone camera, that means a long, decorated front with domes, set against open sky. The road and the wide Marina promenade give you room to stand back and fit it all in.

A good view is from Kamarajar Salai, on the beach side of the road, looking west. From there you see the front facade and domes across the road, with the beach and promenade in the foreground. The front of the building faces the sea, so this is the side most people want. Marina Beach itself is a good second spot. From the sand you get a wider view, with the Senate House rising behind the road.

The building was restored and reopened to the public in 2006. Traffic and passers-by will be in the foreground, so take a few frames and pick the one with the cleanest gap. Whether you can go inside may change, so confirm with the university before visiting.
text.geographic_location: In Chennai, on Wallajah Road along Marina Beach, within the University of Madras campus. The best photo spot is on the beach side of Kamarajar Salai, the Marina's main road.
text.directions_text: No stations or stops are listed near this spot. Head to Kamarajar Salai, the main road along the Marina, and get to the beach side of the road. Take care crossing the road if you want a closer look. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole facade and domes. Switch to the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the domes and carved details. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of beach and promenade in the foreground, as it will make the building look smaller and push its edges outwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Kamarajar Salai (beach side of the road, facing west toward the building). The Senate House's front facade and domes across the road, with the Marina beach and promenade in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the building up with the lower third, leaving the sky above the domes. Keep the phone level so the facade does not lean. Include a strip of promenade or sand in the foreground for depth. For a wider view with the building rising behind the road, try Marina Beach instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky stays blue and the facade keeps its detail. If cars pass in your shot, try a Live Photo and choose the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is a good bet, as the sun should light the sea-facing front. Late afternoon may leave the front in shade, so check the light when you arrive.

text.access_note: The facade can be photographed from the public road and beach, but the building belongs to the university, so confirm with the university before visiting if you want to go inside.
